title: Addresses: how a machine is found
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read an IPv4 address as the 32-bit number it is, tell a private range from a public one, and explain what a netmask actually selects.

blocks.text: An IPv4 address looks like four numbers with dots between them. It is one 32-bit integer, and the dots exist only so people can read it. Almost every confusing thing about addressing becomes obvious once you hold that fact.

blocks.caption: The same address, two ways of writing it
lines: /* Each of the four parts is one byte, so each is 0-255.
That is why 192.168.1.256 is not a typo you can fix — it does not exist. */

blocks.text: An address carries two things at once: which network, and which machine on it. The netmask says where the boundary is. Written as /24 it means the first 24 bits identify the network and the remaining 8 identify the host. The same information is often written the long way, as 255.255.255.0, which is simply 24 one-bits followed by 8 zero-bits.

blocks.title: Why two addresses are always unusable
blocks.text: The lowest address in a range identifies the network itself, and the highest is the broadcast address for it. Neither can be given to a machine, which is why a /24 offers 254 hosts rather than 256. Those four rows were computed rather than recalled — the arithmetic is in the exercise, and doing it once is faster than memorising a table.

Three private ranges are reserved for use inside networks, plus the loopback range for this machine itself. The three private ranges are not routed on the internet, so anyone may use them, and almost everyone does; loopback never leaves the machine at all.

rows: Loopback: this machine, never leaves it

blocks.title: Private addresses appear inside the internet too
blocks.text: Run a traceroute to a public address and you will often see 10.x addresses among the intermediate hops. Those are the provider's own internal links — private ranges used inside their network, which is entirely legitimate. It surprises people who expect every hop on the internet to be publicly addressable. What matters is that no one can route to those addresses from outside that provider.

blocks.caption: An interface and what each part means
lines: netmask   /24             <- the first 24 bits are the network
broadcast 192.0.2.255     <- address OR the inverted mask
range     192.0.2.1 to 192.0.2.254 are available for machines
/* Anything inside that range is reached directly on this segment.
Anything outside it is sent to the gateway — the next lesson. */

blocks.text: The addresses in that example are from a block reserved for documentation, which is why they are safe to publish. When you run the command on your own machine you will see your real ones, and you should treat them the way you would any other detail about your network.

blocks.title: Read your own address as a number
steps: Run: ip addr show     (or ifconfig on macOS) and find your address and netmask
Convert your address to binary by hand, one byte at a time
Apply the mask: keep the bits the mask has as 1, zero the rest — that is your network
Invert the mask and OR it in — that is your broadcast address
Check your arithmetic: ipcalc <address>/<prefix>   if it is installed, or a calculator
Run: ping -c 1 <your broadcast address>    and see whether anything answers
Work out how many usable addresses your network has, then run: ip neigh   to see how many are in use
Run: traceroute -n 1.1.1.1   and look for private ranges among the hops
blocks.expected: A network and broadcast address you derived yourself and then confirmed, and a traceroute that probably contains 10.x addresses partway along. Doing the bit arithmetic by hand once is what makes the next lesson's subnetting straightforward rather than a memorisation exercise.

cheatsheet: An IPv4 address is one 32-bit number; the dots are for humans
Each part is one byte, so 0-255 — anything above 255 is not an address
A prefix like /24 says how many leading bits identify the network
255.255.255.0 is the same thing as /24 written the long way
network = address AND mask; broadcast = address OR inverted mask
Two addresses per range are unusable: the network and the broadcast
Private addresses inside a traceroute are the provider's internal links, not an error

checkpoint.prompt: How many addresses can be assigned to machines in a /26?
checkpoint.explanation: A /26 leaves 6 host bits, so 64 addresses, minus the network address and the broadcast address. This was computed rather than recalled — the same arithmetic gives 254 for a /24 and 4094 for a /20.

checkpoint.prompt: A traceroute to a public server shows 10.x.x.x addresses at hops 3 and 4. What does that mean?

choices.A: A misconfiguration of the routing table on your machine
choices.D: Those are the provider's internal links

checkpoint.explanation: Private ranges are unroutable from outside, but perfectly usable inside a provider's network. Seeing them mid-path is normal and tells you nothing is wrong. They use private addressing inside the provider's own network, which is perfectly normal.

checkpoint.prompt: What does a netmask actually do?

choices.D: Limits how many machines may connect

checkpoint.explanation: It is a bit pattern of ones followed by zeros. AND it with the address and you have the network; the bits it leaves out are the host part. The network is identified by the leading bits of the address; the bits it leaves out are the host part.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can 192.168.1.256 never be a valid address?

choices.A: Each of the four parts is a single byte
choices.C: It belongs to a different network than the local one

checkpoint.explanation: The largest value any of them can hold is 255. The dotted notation is just a readable form of four bytes. 256 does not fit in a byte, so there is no 32-bit number that would produce it.
